hints: Split the ester at the $\text{C(=O)O}$ group and name the two parts separately, the $\text{OCH}_{3}$ part first as alkyl, then the carbonyl chain as alkanoate.
walkthrough:
See the two halves of the ester**
Look at ester A, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(=O)OCH}_{3}$. Think of it as an acid part joined to an alcohol part. The $\text{OCH}_{3}$ side comes from methanol, so that gives the first word methyl.

Count the acid chain including the carbonyl carbon**
Now count the chain that contains the $\text{C=O}$ carbon. There are 5 carbons in a straight line including that carbonyl carbon, so the parent acid is pentanoic acid. For an ester this becomes pentanoate. Put them together to get methyl pentanoate.

hints: Think about the journey of one ester through the column, from the moment it enters to the moment the detector sees it.
walkthrough:
Picture what happens in the column**
Imagine you inject the mixture. Each ester sticks to the stationary phase and moves with the carrier gas to a different extent, so they arrive at the detector at different times. Retention time is simply how long one component spends in the whole process.

Pin down start and finish**
The clock starts when you inject the sample onto the column and stops when that particular ester reaches the detector and gives its peak. That time delay is characteristic and is used to identify the ester.
Final answer: time between injection (of sample onto column) and detection (of component leaving column)

hints: Recall that peak area is proportional to mass, so add all four peak areas to find the total that represents 100%.
walkthrough:
Turn areas into a total mass scale**
You are told area is proportional to mass, so you can treat areas like masses. Add them: $14 + 25 + 52 + 38 = 129$. That 129 represents the total mass of mixture.

Pick out ester D**
Ester D has area 38. So its fraction is $$\frac{38}{129}$$ Multiply by 100 to get percent: $$\frac{38}{129} \times 100 = 29.46\%$$ which rounds to $29.5\%$ to three significant figures, matching the data.

Final answer: percentage by mass of ester D = 29.5%
$$\frac{38}{14+25+52+38} \times 100 = 29.5\%$$

hints: For each ester, label every $\text{H}$ and $\text{C}$ and look for symmetry, remembering that the two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups in $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ are equivalent but all groups in ester B are different.
Count unique proton environments and unique carbon environments separately, remembering $\text{OCH}_{3}$ is always its own environment in both spectra.
walkthrough:
Work through ester B atom by atom**
Write B as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)OCH}_{3}$. For protons: the ethyl $\text{CH}_{3}$, the ethyl $\text{CH}_{2}$, the $\text{CH}$, the branched $\text{CH}_{3}$, and the $\text{OCH}_{3}$ are all in different surroundings. That is 5 proton environments. For carbons: $\text{C=O}$, $\text{OCH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}$, branched $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$, ethyl $\text{CH}_{3}$ are all different. That is 6 carbon environments.

Work through ester C and spot the symmetry**
Write C as $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{C(=O)OCH}_{3}$. The two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups attached to the same $\text{CH}$ are identical by symmetry, so they give one proton signal together. Then you have $\text{CH}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$ and $\text{OCH}_{3}$. That is $1+1+1+1 = 4$ proton peaks. For carbons, the two equivalent $\text{CH}_{3}$ carbons give one peak, plus $\text{CH}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$, $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{OCH}_{3}$. That is 5 carbon peaks.

Final answer: ester B: 5 peaks in proton ($^{1}\text{H}$) NMR; 6 peaks in carbon-13 NMR
ester C: 4 peaks in proton ($^{1}\text{H}$) NMR; 5 peaks in carbon-13 NMR

hints: Remember a triplet means the protons have exactly two equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon or carbons ($n+1 = 3$).
walkthrough:
Translate triplet into structure**
A triplet tells you there is a proton group next to a $\text{CH}_{2}$ group (2 neighbours). Look for a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}$ or $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}$ fragment.

Check A to D quickly**
Ester A, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, has several $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to $\text{CH}_{2}$ and a terminal $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{CH}_{2}$, so it must show triplets. Ester B, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, has $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}$, so that $\text{CH}_{3}$ is a triplet. Ester C, $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, has $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{CH}$ (doublet) and $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to $\text{CH}$ (doublet), no triplet. Ester D, $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{3}\text{CCO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, has only singlets. So only A and B qualify.

hints: Use the two starting clues for F, effervescence with $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ and stereoisomerism, to deduce it must contain $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{C=C}$.
Use the iodoform result, yellow $\text{CHI}_{3}$ plus H, to deduce F must contain a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)}$ group and work out the remaining $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$ skeleton.
Recall that $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ reduces $\text{C=O}$ in ketones and acids to alcohols but leaves $\text{C=C}$ untouched, to predict J.
Recall that $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ converts only $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{COCl}$ to predict K.
Think of L as a normal esterification of the acyl chloride K with propan-2-ol, replacing $\text{Cl}$ by $\text{OCH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$.

Check each formula given ($\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{2}$, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{7}\text{O}_{2}\text{Cl}$) to confirm your H counts and that H is the dicarboxylic acid left after loss of $\text{CHI}_{3}$.
walkthrough:
Decode F from three clues**
Effervescence with $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}(aq)$ means F is a carboxylic acid, it has $\text{COOH}$. Stereoisomerism with formula $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$ means it has a $\text{C=C}$ that can show E/Z isomerism, so each C of the double bond must have two different groups. Positive iodoform means it has $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)}$. Put these together and count atoms: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)OH}$ gives $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$ exactly and fits all three tests.

Split F with alkaline iodine**
The reaction is: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)R + I}_{2} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{CHI}_{3} + \text{RCOO}^{-}$$ So G is the yellow precipitate triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_{3}$. The rest of F, $\text{CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)COOH}$, becomes a carboxylate and on work up the diacid H: $\text{HOOCCH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)COOH}$, which is 2-methylbut-2-enedioic acid.

Reduce F with $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ to get J**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is a strong reducing agent. It reduces the ketone $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)}$ to a secondary alcohol $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$ and the acid $\text{COOH}$ to a primary alcohol $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, but it does not touch the $\text{C=C}$. So J is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, formula $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{2}$ as given.

Convert the acid to the acyl chloride K**
$\text{SOCl}_{2}$ replaces $\text{OH}$ of the carboxylic acid by $\text{Cl}$: $$\text{RCOOH + SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{RCOCl + SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$$ The ketone and alkene are unchanged. So K is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)Cl}$, formula $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{7}\text{O}_{2}\text{Cl}$.

Make the isopropyl ester L**
Acyl chloride plus alcohol gives ester plus HCl: $$\text{RCOCl + (CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHOH} \rightarrow \text{RCOOCH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2} + \text{HCl}$$ So replace $\text{Cl}$ in K by $\text{OCH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$. L is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)OCH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$, the propan-2-yl ester.

Final answer: F: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)OH}$
G: $\text{CHI}_{3}$
H: $\text{HOC(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)OH}$
J: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$
K: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)Cl}$
L: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH=C(CH}_{3}\text{)C(=O)OCH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$
